nameStory: The 'seedcorn' in this beetle's common name comes from their habit of feeding on crop seeds, particularly corn kernels that have been planted but haven't yet sprouted. While farmers sometimes consider them pests, these beetles actually eat many other small seeds and help control weed populations. The scientific name 'ochropezus' refers to their yellowish legs - 'ochro' meaning yellow-brown and 'pezus' meaning foot.
description: Stenolophus ochropezus is a small ground beetle that scurries along the soil surface hunting for seeds and tiny prey. These compact beetles typically measure about 4-6mm long (roughly the size of a large grain of rice) with an oval, somewhat flattened body. They have a dark brown to black head and thorax with lighter brown wing covers, and their legs are distinctly yellowish-brown. Like all ground beetles, they're fast runners that prefer to dash away rather than fly when disturbed.

idTips.label: Yellowish legs
idTips.description: The legs are noticeably pale yellow-brown or amber colored, contrasting sharply with the darker body - this is often the first feature you'll notice as they scurry away

idTips.label: Size and shape
idTips.description: Small and oval-shaped, about the length of your pinky nail, with a slightly flattened appearance that helps them slip under debris

idTips.label: Color pattern
idTips.description: Dark brownish-black head and thorax with lighter brown wing covers that may have a slight metallic sheen in good light

idTips.label: Movement style
idTips.description: Extremely quick runners that dart in zigzag patterns when disturbed - they rarely fly and prefer to dash under the nearest cover

idTips.label: Antennae
idTips.description: Thread-like antennae that are constantly moving and twitching as they explore their surroundings, about half the length of their body

idTips.label: Texture
idTips.description: Hard, smooth wing covers with very fine parallel grooves that you can feel with your fingertip if you manage to catch one

habitat: Look for these beetles in agricultural areas, gardens, and disturbed soils where seeds are abundant - they're particularly common around corn fields, vegetable gardens, and weedy areas. They prefer moist, loose soil where they can easily burrow and hunt for fallen seeds. You'll often find them under rocks, boards, or garden mulch during the day, and active on bare soil surfaces at dusk.

seasonality.spring: Adults become active as soil warms, often found under garden debris or mulch. This is when they're most likely to be discovered in newly planted garden beds.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period when adults are most visible hunting on soil surfaces at dawn and dusk. Look for them around outdoor lights at night where they may be drawn to hunt other small insects.
seasonality.fall: Still active but beginning to seek overwintering sites under deeper debris, logs, or in soil crevices. Often found when turning over garden compost or leaf litter.
seasonality.winter: Adults hibernate under rocks, logs, or deep in soil. Occasionally found when digging in unfrozen soil during warm spells.

funFact: These tiny beetles are actually helping your garden in a sneaky way - while they do eat some crop seeds, they consume far more weed seeds, essentially working as unpaid garden assistants that patrol your soil 24/7 eating the seeds of plants you don't want!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with the Lined Stenolophus, but that species has distinct light stripes running lengthwise down its wing covers, while ochropezus has more uniformly colored wings. Memory trick: 'Lined has lines, ochropezus is plain' - if you see stripes, it's the other species.
contextualKnowledge: Don't let the 'pest' reputation fool you - while agricultural guides sometimes list seedcorn beetles as crop pests, they're actually beneficial in most garden settings. The concern mainly applies to large-scale corn farming where they might eat newly planted seeds before sprouting.
compareHints: Compared to its close relative the Lined Stenolophus, ochropezus lacks the distinctive pale stripes on the wing covers and tends to be slightly more uniformly dark. Both species have the characteristic yellowish legs, but only the Lined Stenolophus has those telltale light-colored lines running down its back. In the broader ground beetle family, seedcorn beetles are much smaller and more seed-focused than the larger predatory species like the common black ground beetles.

relatedSpecies.distinction: The Lined Stenolophus differs from its close relative Stenolophus ochropezus primarily in the visibility of its pale wing stripes - ochropezus tends to have more uniform coloring without distinct lines.
